title: Crafted by Curiosity
description: A reflection on how children’s creativity, persistence, and love for hands-on learning reveal something deeply human. From crochet to glitter-covered chargers, their willingness to keep improving shows that growth comes through practice, challenge, and imperfect attempts—and that in an age of AI, skills built through our own hands, patience, and experience still hold unique value.
full_description:
My elder daughter picked up crocheting a few weeks back and she's glued to it. Meanwhile, my younger daughter discovered her own canvas. Every charger in the house or glasses. Glittery beads, glue and whatever design inspires her that day transform chargers into her art project, one dazzling layer at a time.

What struck me most is that neither of them stopped at good enough (or it seems). My elder daughter progressed beyond basic stitches into designs / art work within weeks. My younger one continually upgrades her art, adding more sparkle, detail and her own unique touch. They’re driven by the challenge itself.

There’s a psychological explanation for this. Research on motivation reveals that achieving a goal triggers a reward in the brain. This reward not only feels good but also motivates us to seek out more difficult challenges. Success or meeting your goal doesn’t lead to complacency; it pushes us to grow and stretch.

Watching them transition from let me try this to look what I made prompted me to think and write about this.

They manage all this alongside school and hifz; Alhmadulillah, memorising the Qur’an, keeping up with their studies and still finding time for yarn, glue and glitter. Both fought for this time and learned something few classrooms teach these days. How to build something with your hands, imperfectly at first, then improving and ultimately creating something beautiful.

This brings me to a larger perspective. Our mothers and grandmothers were skilled in handcrafts such as crochet, sewing and cooking. We were instead drawn into classrooms, where school became the AI of our generation, standardising skills that had been passed down through families. Decades later, the very thing that replaced our grandmothers’ skills (education, structured knowledge, schools) is being replaced by actual AI

Crochet, carpentry, plumbing and even a glitter-covered charger; these still belong to us. It’s not because AI can’t eventually master them but because they’re built on something slower: dexterity and muscle memory honed through countless imperfect attempts. My daughters aren’t simply decorating yarn and chargers. They’re demonstrating that the drive to grow and strive for greater heights remains theirs to experience and achieve.

title: Overthinking in business
description:
Things I used to overthink as a business owner… that don’t carry the same weight anymore.

How will clients come? How will we sustain expenses?

At the beginning, these questions felt heavy. Almost like they needed to be answered completely before taking a single step.

But now, looking back, I realize something deeper:
We were never fully in control of those answers to begin with.
full_description:
I've been reflecting on this thought lately:

Destiny doesn't reveal itself all at once. It reveals itself only to those who have the patience to keep walking.

When people hear the word sabr, they often imagine waiting.

Doing nothing.
Enduring until life changes.
But I see patience differently.

Patience is not the absence of action. It is continuing to act when the outcome refuses to reveal itself. When we started TRPL Solutions there was a project we almost didn't take. It was bigger than anything we had built before.

We questioned ourselves. Were we ready? Did we have enough experience? Could we actually deliver?

Confidence said, "Not yet."
Tawakkul said, "Take the next step."

So we did. Not because we knew how everything would unfold.

But because we believed that our responsibility was the effort, not the outcome. Months later, that same project is nearing completion.

Looking back, I don't think confidence came before the journey. The journey gave me confidence. That seems to be how Allah teaches us. The path rarely becomes visible before we begin walking. It reveals itself one step at a time.

The same is true with people. Clients sometimes delay payments because they're carrying burdens you cannot see. Colleagues make mistakes while fighting battles they never speak about.

Sometimes the easiest response is to react. To replace. To walk away.

But I've learned that patience is also a form of belief. Belief that people can grow. Belief that trust, once invested wisely, often bears fruit later than expected.

Without tawakkul, patience feels like carrying a weight. With tawakkul, patience is a strategy.

You stop demanding that life explain itself immediately. You begin trusting that some answers only arrive with time.

Perhaps that is why so much of life only makes sense in retrospect.

The delays.
The disappointments.
The unexpected turns.

None of them seemed meaningful while they were happening. Yet looking back, they formed a path I could never have designed myself.

Maybe destiny is not something we discover at the end. Maybe it is something that quietly reveals itself to those who refuse to stop walking.

And perhaps that is what patience has been all along.

title: What truly drives performance
description: In business, we rely heavily on numbers: revenue targets, utilisation rates, margins, cashflow, cost controls etc.. In our business of IT enabled products, we engineer entire systems around measurement. Numbers give direction. Money provides fuel. Without them, organisations cannot survive, let alone grow. However, observing around I realised that two busineses may have similar credentials, tools, and frameworks.

title: Between momentum & meaning
description: Business is growing, responsibility has increased, and there’s clarity of purpose (or it seems). There’s a quiet sense of contentment in that. And yet, alongside it, there’s also conflict. Not the kind of conflict driven by fear or instability. This is a different tension, one between momentum and meaning.
full_description:
Between momentum & meaning

Business is growing, responsibility has increased, and there’s clarity of purpose (or it seems). There’s a quiet sense of contentment in that. And yet, alongside it, there’s also conflict. Not the kind of conflict driven by fear or instability. This is a different tension, one between momentum and meaning.

Over the years I have become more aware of how growth changes everything. Responsibility deepens, and with it comes the weight of knowing that your choices now affect more lives than just your own.

What I didn’t expect was how easily speed begins to crowd out depth. Not through bad intentions, but through small, reasonable compromises made in the name of efficiency. That’s when I started feeling unsure, not about direction, but about growth.

What worries me isn’t failure. It’s the possibility of success that quietly erodes the very values that made the journey meaningful in the first place. The fear that growth, if left unchecked, can dilute quality, thoughtfulness, honesty, and presence (or is success even success without values or meaning?).

Stability comes with its own questions. What do you optimise for when fear or need is no longer driving you? That’s where integrity is really tested, not in hardship, but in momentum.

I’m learning that responsibility isn’t about carrying everything. It’s about deciding what must not be compromised as complexity grows. Protecting quality when speed is rewarded. Protecting truth when silence is easier. Protecting people around you.

I don’t have this fully figured out yet. I’m still learning where to pause and where to push, how to lead without being consumed, how to grow without becoming someone I wouldn’t want to work for.

But one thing feels increasingly clear a business can grow faster than the inner life of the person leading it and that gap if left unchecked is dangerous and is often recognised only when its too late.

Right now, my focus isn’t only on scaling systems or revenue. It’s on scaling without losing alignment with values, with clarity, with the reasons I started at all.

title: Your rizq is already written for you
description:
Your rizq is already written for you, and Allah will never abandon you.

I founded my software company last year, and it has been about 13 months of building since then. And I’ve slowly started to internalize is this. We were never meant to carry the burden of how our provision will come because that was never in our control to begin with.
full_description:
Your rizq is already written for you, and Allah will never abandon you.

I founded my software company last year, and it has been about 13 months of building since then. And I’ve slowly started to internalize is this:

We were never meant to carry the burden of how our provision will come because that was never in our control to begin with.

We tried to never worry about clients the way most people assume a business should.

Not because everything was easy but because somewhere deep inside, there is a conviction that provision does not come from certainty of plans; it comes from the One who writes it.

And yet, I see how easily people forget this. Even I do, at times.

We overestimate planning and underestimate decree. We believe clarity must come before action, when often clarity only reveals itself through action.

When I speak to someone thinking about starting a business, I tell them this:

Take action. Begin.

You can choose what you will do, and why you will do it. But the how - the path, the opening, the rizq - that is not yours to engineer (to an extent).

It unfolds in ways you could not design, even if you tried.

Start with good Niyyah as it is the direction of everything that follows.

And tawakkul is not passive thinking.

It is doing everything within your capacity; research, planning, structure, effort and then releasing the illusion that control ever belonged to you.

Yet many people remain stuck at the stage of planning. As if certainty is a requirement before action. But life rarely gives certainty first.

We think. We plan. And then we step forward not because we see the entire path, but because we trust the One who does.

That, for me, is what building a business has slowly taught me.

How to let go of the need to control what was never mine to control in the first place.

title: Children grow up fast
description:
I remember my eldest daughter being born with remarkable clarity. I can still picture every little detail. The tiny person trying to make sense of a new world, looking around with curious eyes. 

She would fall asleep on my chest, and today she is almost as tall as I am.
full_description:
Children grow up fast…

I remember my eldest daughter being born with remarkable clarity. I can still picture every little detail. The tiny person trying to make sense of a new world, looking around with curious eyes.

She would fall asleep on my chest, and today she is almost as tall as I am.

Children grow up fast, Alhamdulillah. The strange thing is, you rarely notice it while it’s happening. Life keeps us busy. Days become weeks, weeks become years, and one day you find yourself wondering where it all went.

Very early on, I decided that no matter how demanding life became, I wanted to be present. I traded a comfortable job for one with greater uncertainty because it gave me the opportunity to build something while spending more time with my children. Looking back, I have never regretted that decision.

Every summer holiday has become a tradition. We go shopping together for the new school year, uniforms, books, shoes, and stationery. There is always the official list of things we need. But the real shopping begins once we step into the store.

The school shoes somehow become school shoes plus a pair of sandals. A notebook becomes a sparkly diary. A pen becomes the one with glitter. Somehow, the list grows with every aisle we walk through. And once the shopping is done, there is an unwritten tradition that is just as important: snacks, ice cream, or whatever wasn’t on the official list.

These are the moments I find myself cherishing more with every passing year.

I smile as they carefully plan how to “rob” me of my money. Their mother reminds me that I need to set boundaries. My own mother tells me everything is getting too expensive and that I should spend carefully. Everyone is simply playing their part, and I have to play mine not just as a provider, but as a father who is present.

To be there.

To listen. And, as my daughters insist, sometimes to listen without turning everything into a lecture.

Parenthood is a delicate balance. When our children are young, we are often in the busiest and most demanding phase of our lives. Building careers, paying bills, chasing stability. Ironically, those are also the years that disappear the fastest. By the time we realise how quickly time is passing, childhood is already slipping through our fingers.

That is why these summer holidays mean so much to me. They are not always extraordinary vacations. They are simple days spent together, eating ice cream, laughing over unnecessary purchases, and having conversations that I hope my children will remember long after they’ve forgotten what we actually bought.

As we grow older, many of us begin to appreciate what our own fathers quietly did for us, often with far fewer resources than we have today. We realise that happiness was never really about how much money was spent. It was about presence. About sacrifice. About showing up.

May Allah make our children the coolness of our eyes, and may He make us the coolness of our parents’ eyes. Ameen.

title: Viewing uncertainty in business
description: A reflection on the first year of entrepreneurship and the deeper lessons it brings, learning to live with uncertainty, practice confidence, build trust, and grow alongside the business you’re creating.
full_description:
I started TRPL Solutions last July and people often ask me what the first year taught me.

They expect lessons about sales, hiring, software, and scaling. Those lessons came. But the deeper lessons are harder to explain because they don't change the business.

They change the person running it.

This year taught me that uncertainty is not a phase of entrepreneurship. It is the environment in which founders learn to live.

→  You make decisions without certainty
→  You commit before you feel ready
→  You solve problems you've never seen before

And somewhere along the way, you stop asking, "When will this become easier?" Instead, you begin asking, "Who must I become to carry this well?"

That question changed everything for me. I realised that confidence is not the absence of doubt.

Some days I felt capable of building anything. Other days I questioned whether I belonged in the room at all. Both emotions visited me. Neither stayed for long.

Perhaps confidence isn't something founders possess. Perhaps it's something they practice.

I also realized that businesses are built on something far less visible than code or capital.

They are built on trust.

Every moment you choose honesty over convenience. Those small decisions quietly become your reputation. And over time, your reputation becomes the business.

I don't think entrepreneurship changes people.

I think it exposes them.

It shows you who you are when the answers are unclear, when the pressure is real, and when no one is coming to solve the problem for you.

One year later, I'm grateful for the company we've built.

But I'm even more grateful for the person the journey is slowly teaching me to become.

Because maybe that's the real work.

We think we're building businesses. All along, they're quietly building us.

Here's to year two. To continue building with more wisdom than certainty, more patience than speed, and more integrity than ambition.

title: Reputation is everything
description:
Revenue is important but reputation is everything. In the beginning, revenue seems to be the primary driving force in business. 

More clients. More projects. More growth.
full_description:
The longer I build, the more convinced I become of this:

Revenue is important but reputation is everything.

In the beginning, revenue seems to be the primary driving force in business.

More clients. More projects. More growth.

And of course, revenue matters. A business cannot survive without it. But over time, I realized something deeper:

Revenue is a transaction. Reputation is a memory.

Revenue appears on your statements. Reputation lives in the minds of people long after the work is done.

A client will eventually forget the invoice amount. But they will remember how you made them feel. They will remember whether you kept your word.

Whether you were honest when things went wrong. Whether you chose integrity when it was expensive.

Business may seem like an exchange of money but at its core it is an exchange of trust.

And trust is strange. It takes years to build. Moments to lose. And once broken, it rarely returns in its original form.

The older I get, the more I realize that reputation compounds in much the same way character does.

Every small decision leaves a trace.

Every promise kept.

Every difficult conversation handled with honesty.

Every moment where you choose what is right over what is easy.

These moments seem insignificant when they happen. But over time, they become your name.

And in many ways, a person's name is their greatest asset. Because markets change. Industries evolve. Businesses come and go. But people never forget who you were when circumstances tested you.

Perhaps this is why I no longer see reputation as a business strategy. I see it as a way of living.

Revenue may sustain a business for a season. But reputation is what allows it to outlive the season itself.

What do you think compounds faster over a lifetime: money or reputation?

title: Nourishing the soul
description: A reflection on redefining success through the lens of the Hereafter—where sincere intention, meaningful effort, and obedience matter more than outcomes. It also explores how this perspective can reshape parenting, priorities, and the way we value our limited time.
full_description:
I’ve realized that one of the things occupying most of my thoughts is parenting, raising children in a way that gives them the best chance of succeeding not just in this life, but in the Hereafter.

I’ve been listening to The Afterlife Manual by Ousama Alshurafa and it has been one of the most thought provoking books I’ve come across.

It answers basic questions many of us carry but rarely find answers to: the reality of means (asbab) the true definition of success, the value of time, and how our perspective on life, relationships, work, and business changes when viewed through the lens of the Hereafter.

One idea, in particular, has stayed with me.

We often think of success as a destination, a promotion, a thriving business, financial freedom, or achieving a particular milestone. But the book presents success differently.

Success is not a point you eventually reach. Success exists in the present. Every action done sincerely for the sake of Allah and in accordance with His guidance is already a success, regardless of the outcome. Outcomes belong to Allah. Our responsibility is our intention, effort, and obedience.

That single shift in perspective changes everything. It removes much of the anxiety we create for ourselves by constantly chasing future achievements that were never meant to be chased. It reminds us that perhaps we have complicated our lives far more than they were ever meant to be.

Another lesson that resonated deeply was the value of time. Time is our only true capital. Once it is spent, it can never be earned back.

I’m not finished with the book yet, but it has already reshaped many of my thoughts about parenting, priorities, and what it really means to live a successful life.

We need more books and content like this. Many Muslims, especially the younger generation, seem either directionless or fixated on goals that were never meant to be the ultimate pursuit. A return to first principles, to understanding our purpose, redefining success, and viewing this life through the lens of the Hereafter may be one of the greatest gifts we can give ourselves and our children.

title: Importance of building systems for founders
description:
Passion might build things and give you a good start but systems sustain them.

In the beginning, I believed passion and hard work could compensate for almost anything. And to some extent, they can. When you're small, energy hides inefficiency. You work longer hours, respond faster, and carry more yourself.
full_description:
Passion builds. Systems endure.

Passion might build things and give you a good start but systems sustain them.

In the beginning, I believed passion and hard work could compensate for almost anything. And to some extent, they can. When you're small, energy hides inefficiency. You work longer hours, respond faster, and carry more yourself.

Founders become the systems. But eventually, that approach begins to reveal its limits.

Because human beings are inconsistent. We get tired. We forget. We become overwhelmed.

And businesses built solely on human effort inherit that same fragility. That's when I started thinking differently. A system, at its core, is simply a way of preserving intention. It ensures that promises are kept even when motivation fades.

That clients receive updates even on difficult days. That quality remains consistent regardless of mood, pressure, or circumstance.

Without systems, a business becomes dependent on memory. With systems, it is backed by principles. The same principles that the passion built in the first place.

And perhaps that is true beyond business too. Much of life itself is sustained through systems.

Prayer times.
Routines.
Habits.

Small disciplines repeated consistently over time. We often admire extraordinary moments, yet most meaningful things are built through ordinary actions performed repeatedly.

The same applies to companies. Founders often believe they need to work harder. Sometimes what they really need is to think more deeply about what should no longer depend on them.

Because businesses do not truly mature when the founder becomes indispensable. They mature when the founder becomes unnecessary for the routine things.

The first year of building taught me this:

Hustle creates momentum. But systems create permanence. And permanence is what allows something to outlive the energy of the person who started it.

What system in your business or life has had the biggest impact on you?

title: Character
description: True character of a team isn’t revealed when everything goes according to plan; it’s revealed when almost nothing does.
full_description:
True character of a team isn’t revealed when everything goes according to plan; it’s revealed when almost nothing does.

We signed a software development contract with a three-month timeline. We were excited. Confident. Ready to prove ourselves.

Looking back, we made mistakes. The project was underpriced. The scope was more complex than we initially understood. And perhaps most importantly, the team we assigned wasn't yet the right team for the challenge ahead.

Like many founders in the early stages, I believed effort could compensate for  gaps. Sometimes it does. Sometimes it’s not that simple.

As development progressed, a difficult truth became impossible to ignore.

The product we were building was not the product we wanted our name attached to.

Although the product worked. It solved the problem. But deep down, we knew it wasn't right. And that realization created a choice.

Do we deliver something that technically meets the requirements and move on? Or do we accept the cost of our own misjudgment and rebuild from a stronger foundation? We chose the latter, to rebuild.

The interesting part of the story isn't what we did. It's what the client did.

They trusted us.

Because they saw that we cared about the outcome more than protecting our ego.

They could have asked for a refund. Honestly, we were prepared to give it. Instead, they gave us something far more valuable. A second chance. And second chances are strange. They rarely appear in contracts. They appear in relationships.

The second version was better in every way. Cleaner. More thoughtful. Built with greater clarity.

The client loved it. So much so, they signed us to build an entire mobile application on top of the same system.

What began as our weakest project became one of our strongest relationships.

And over time, I realized something:

Most founders fear failure. But failure is rarely the thing that destroys trust.

Avoiding responsibility does. The first version of almost anything in life is most likely to be flawed.

That project taught me something I don't think business books explain very well:

Clients always remember how you behaved when things stopped going according to plan. And perhaps that's true beyond business too.

To the clients who give second chances. Thank you.

You often have no idea how much growth exists on the other side of your patience.

title: Raising children
description: I am raising my 2 children differently. People tell me my approach is wrong. They go to school while doing Hifz. The modern world often makes it feel like you must choose.  And somewhere along the way, we accepted the idea that raising children must become a choice between dunya and deen making them mutually exclusive.

title: Minimum Viable Product [MVP]
description: Build a product based on the minimum requirements needed to solve the client’s problem.

title: The biggest lesson I learned in building my company
description: We didn’t ignore preparation entirely. In many ways, we did what any finance-oriented founder would do. We built feasibility studies, projections, and market studies.
full_description:
The biggest lesson I learned in the first 3 months of building my company

Not what you might expect.

Not a bad product, neither the wrong timing nor a difficult market.

We didn’t ignore preparation entirely. In many ways, we did what any finance-oriented founder would do. We built feasibility studies, projections, and market studies.

On paper, we were good to go. But we missed the part that mattered most. Structure.

I hired developers. Only developers. The best I could.

When you believe in an idea deeply enough, there’s a quiet pull to just begin. To build. To move. That energy isn’t wrong.

But conviction without preparation is just enthusiasm with a timeline.

At the time, it seemed logical.

We were a software company, so naturally the focus went into building software. But I had confused the product with the foundation of the business itself.

A business isn’t only what it creates. It’s how it sells, how it supports its people, and how it thinks about tomorrow while delivering today.

The gap showed up quickly.

We had capability without structure. Technical depth without operational clarity. The ability to deliver, but not yet the foundation to grow.

What I didn’t fully understand then was this:

A team reflects the assumptions of its founder.

I assumed we would figure the rest out later. The team assumed the same. And for a while, momentum carried us forward until it no longer could.

10 months in, I’m still correcting that early imbalance. Slowly. Deliberately. One honest conversation and one right hire at a time.

The lesson isn’t that urgency was wrong.

It’s that urgency without enough homework doesn’t save time. It simply shifts the cost to a later stage, where it becomes heavier, harder, and far more personal.

The idea deserved more than excitement.

It deserved full attention before the first line of code was written.

title: Are customised softwares a thing of the past?
description: It’s undeniable that off-the-shelf software solutions can serve many businesses well, especially when quick setup and basic functionality are sufficient. However, when organizations seek real competitive advantage or need to address unique business challenges, customised software remains irreplaceable.

title: What We Take Back from Umrah
description:
A reflection on Umrah as more than a physical journey to the Kaaba .
it is a journey of the heart toward Allah. The true measure of the pilgrimage may not be in reaching Makkah, but in returning home spiritually changed.
full_description:
What do we take back from Umrah?

Traveling for Umrah is becoming popular every year. More and more people come, driven by love, longing, and the desire to see the Kaaba & pray in the Prophet’s ﷺ mosque.

On my last trip I came back with a few take aways as to improve on my return. Checked a few things and missed a few. These included Sunnahs I noticed that Arab muslims have kept alive such as using miswak and fasting (Mondays & Thursdays). This time was different..

This visit inspired me to work on my heart. The hearts’ journey to the Lord of Kaaba like the bodys’ journey to the Kaaba.

Makkah physically tires you. It is always happening almost without pause. The Tawaf keeps you moving. The crowd sails. You walk, pray, wait, return, and walk again. At times, you almost forget yourself. Any such activity like this would probably put me to bed at home. But Makkah is different. Somehow, it gives you life. So much so, you forget that it is more about the soul and the heart than of the body. Despite the exhaustion, you want to make another Tawaf. You want to pray again. You want to restart.

But why? What is all of this supposed to teach us? We know the virtues. Sins are wiped clean. Poverty is relieved. Like that of namaz which is supposed to restrain us from shameful and unjust deeds. But does it? Likewise does Umrah actually change us?

We grew up hearing stories of people who went for Hajj or Umrah and came back different. And I wonder what has happened to us? We hear the Qur’an. We pray. We perform Umrah. We stand before the Kaaba. Yet sometimes, we return to exactly the same person we were before we left.

We have become accustomed to hearing beautiful words without allowing them to disturb us. We hear reminders, but rarely let them challenge us. We perform acts of worship, but sometimes they become routines rather than encounters with Allah.

Like Salah, Umrah can become a habit. Even standing before the Kaaba can become something we photograph rather than something that transforms us. And perhaps that is the question we should ask ourselves. What is Allah asking me to become because of this journey? The purpose of coming here cannot simply be to experience Makkah. It must be to take something of Makkah back with us.

Millions may come to Makkah every year. The numbers may continue to rise. But perhaps the real measure of our pilgrimage is not how many people came. It is how many people went back changed.

Gai Eaton in his book “Islam and destiny of man” argues that while Kaaba is the centre of the world for every muslim, it is also a symbol of muslims own inward centre "the heart" where all things come together. He says that the muslim journeys horizontally to Mecca towards Kaaba while the heart journeys vertically to the Lord of Kaaba.

May we leave Makkah physically exhausted, but spiritually renewed. And may we return home carrying something far more precious than just memories: A heart that has been moved by Allah.
